questions.questionText: Figure 1 shows the aggregate demand (AD) and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is most likely to cause aggregate demand to shift from AD1 to AD2 and long-run aggregate supply to shift from LRAS1 to LRAS2?
options: A fall in spending on imports and a rise in productivity
A reduction in exports and an increase in imports of capital goods
An increase in Bank Rate and a reduction in firms’ costs of production
An increase in saving and a rise in government spending on infrastructure

questions.questionText: To reduce the impact of rising inflation, the government cut indirect taxes on several key goods and services and made a one-off payment to all low-income households. Which one of the following diagrams illustrates the most likely impact on the macroeconomy?
Which one of the following diagrams, A, B, C or D, shows the impact on an economy of a permanent reduction in an indirect tax?

An aggregate demand and short-run aggregate supply diagram is used to illustrate the effect of a rise in imports of goods and services into an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following would be shown on the diagram?
options: A leftward movement along the aggregate demand curve
A leftward movement along the short-run aggregate supply curve
A rightward shift of the aggregate demand curve
A rightward shift of the short-run aggregate supply curve

questions.questionText: Figure 2 shows the aggregate demand (AD), short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is the most likely consequence for firms if an increase in government spending shifts the aggregate demand curve from AD to AD2?
options: Increase in spare capacity
Less corporation tax is paid
More goods are exported
Shortages of skilled labour

questions.questionText: Figure 7 shows two long-run aggregate supply curves (LRAS) for an economy. Which one of the following is most likely to explain the shift of the long-run aggregate supply curve from LRAS1 to LRAS2?
options: A reduction in the basic and higher rates of income tax
A reduction in the geographical mobility of labour
An increase in immigration
An increase in imports of goods and services

questions.questionText: In which one of the following situations is an increase in aggregate demand most likely to result in higher inflation?
options: Household savings are increasing
Mortgage interest rates are high
Resources are fully employed
Unemployment is rising

questions.questionText: A government decides to increase the minimum wage at a time when the rest of the world is coming out of recession. These events cause short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) to shift from SRAS1 to SRAS2 and aggregate demand (AD) to shift from AD1 to AD2. If the initial macroeconomic equilibrium is E1, which one of the following diagrams shows the correct new equilibrium E2?
An economy is experiencing deflation and high employment. The most likely cause of this situation is a
options: deficit on the balance of payments.
government budget surplus.
negative demand-side shock.
positive supply-side shock.

questions.questionText: Figure 2 shows the aggregate demand curve (AD), short-run aggregate supply curves (SRAS) and long-run aggregate supply curve (LRAS) for an economy. The short-run aggregate supply curve shifts from SRAS1 to SRAS2. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the resulting increase in real national output?
options: An increase in bank lending to households
An increase in government expenditure
Productivity rising faster than money wages
The action of the multiplier

questions.questionText: Figure 8 shows the aggregate demand curve (AD) and the long-run aggregate supply curves (LRAS) for an economy. A redistribution of government spending from spending on welfare towards the funding of research and development shifts the long-run aggregate supply curve from LRAS1 to LRAS2. Which one of the following is the most likely effect of this policy?
options: A decrease in the number of people who are economically active
An improvement in the balance of payments on current account
An increase in the size of the government’s budget deficit
The creation of a positive output gap

questions.questionText: Figure 1 shows the aggregate demand (AD) and short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves for an economy. Which one of the following combinations of events is most likely to cause the curves to shift from AD1 to AD2 and from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A higher rate of savings and faster labour productivity growth
Faster economic growth abroad and lower world commodity prices
Higher money wages and more household consumption
Lower interest rates and a higher rate of indirect taxes

questions.questionText: A small island economy suffers extensive damage from a hurricane. The following diagrams show aggregate demand (AD), short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) for the economy. Equilibrium before the hurricane is at E1. Which one of the following diagrams shows the most likely position of E2, the equilibrium reached after the hurricane?

Figure 2 shows two aggregate demand (AD1 and AD2) curves and the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve for an economy. Which one of the following is the government most likely to increase if it wishes to use fiscal policy to reduce national output from Y1 to Y2?
options: Infrastructure expenditure
Interest rates
Rates of income tax
The budget deficit

questions.questionText: Figure 4 shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS1 and SRAS2) curves and the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS1 and LRAS2) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is most likely to move the economy from point M to point N?
options: A decrease in the natural rate of unemployment
A loss of consumer and producer confidence
A natural disaster, damaging productive capacity
A rise in factor prices, resulting in cost-push inflation

questions.questionText: Which one of the following diagrams, A, B, C or D, shows the most likely short-run impact on an economy of an improvement in technology in the production process?

Figure 4 shows two aggregate demand (AD1 and AD2) curves and two long-run aggregate supply (LRAS1 and LRAS2) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is the most likely explanation for the movement of the economy from E1 to E2?
options: A decline in the capital stock resulting from a significant decline in bank funding for business investment
An increase in net foreign investment by firms following a reduction in the rate of inflation
An unexpected reduction in the rate of interest following a fall in the rate of inflation
The growth of government borrowing to fund increased expenditure on infrastructure

questions.questionText: Figure 10 shows two aggregate demand (AD1 and AD2) curves and two short-run aggregate supply (SRAS1 and SRAS2) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is the most likely explanation for the movement of the economy from E1 to E2?
options: A depreciation of the currency and an increase in interest rates
A fall in the prices of raw materials and an increase in investment
An increase in exports and the rate of Value Added Tax
An increase in the supply of money and the level of money wages

questions.questionText: Explain how demand-side and supply-side shocks might increase unemployment in an economy.
Figure 1 shows three aggregate demand (AD) curves, a short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and a long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve. In Figure 1, when
options: aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2, cyclical unemployment is likely to be eliminated.
aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD3, the rate of economic growth is equal to (Y3 – Y1).
the economy is producing at Y1, there is a positive output gap.
the economy is producing at Y2, there is no unemployment.

questions.questionText: Figure 7 shows two aggregate demand (AD1 and AD2) curves and two long-run aggregate supply (LRAS1 and LRAS2) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following combinations, A, B, C or D, is most likely to explain the movement of the economy from E1 to E2? An increase in the
options: budget surplus and size of the multiplier.
exchange rate and supply of money.
rate of inflation and positive output gap.
volume of exports and potential output.

questions.questionText: An economy experiences a positive supply-side shock. Other things remaining equal, the impact on the economy is most likely to be
options: higher inflation and faster economic growth.
higher output and lower inflation.
lower employment and slower economic growth.
lower unemployment and a larger budget deficit.

questions.questionText: Figure 1 shows aggregate demand (AD) curves for an economy. Which one of the following is most likely to cause the aggregate demand curve to shift from AD1 to AD2?
options: A fall in imports
A fall in the price level
A reduction in the budget deficit
A rise in the exchange rate

questions.questionText: Figure 2 shows the aggregate demand (AD) curves and short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves for an economy. Which one of the following combinations of events is most likely to cause aggregate demand to shift from AD1 to AD2 and short-run aggregate supply from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A fall in income tax and lower raw material prices
A fall in net exports and higher labour productivity
A rise in money wages and a rise in household saving
An increase in VAT and a rise in household wealth

questions.questionText: Figure 3 shows an economy’s aggregate demand (AD) and short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves. The initial equilibrium price level is at OP1. Which one of the following is most likely to be responsible for both the cost–push and demand-pull inflationary pressures that raise the price level to OP2?
options: A fall in interest rates
A fall in the exchange rate
A rise in direct taxes
A rise in indirect taxes

questions.questionText: Figure 5 shows the aggregate demand (AD) and long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curves for an economy. Which one of the following policies is most likely to have caused aggregate demand to shift from AD1 to AD2, and long-run aggregate supply to shift from LRAS1 to LRAS2?
options: A lower rate of corporation tax
A reduction in the money supply
An increase in state pensions
An increase in the exchange rate

questions.questionText: Economic growth in the US increases from 2% to 5% a year. This is most likely to represent for the UK a
options: negative demand-side shock.
negative supply-side shock.
positive demand-side shock.
positive supply-side shock.

questions.questionText: In the diagram below, as a result of the government implementing a new industrial policy, the long-run aggregate supply curve shifts from LRAS1 to LRAS2 The shift in LRAS suggests that the industrial policy is most likely to have
options: caused firms to be more innovative.
created a positive output gap.
reduced employment and inflation.
reduced imports and exports.

questions.questionText: World oil prices rise by 30%. On an AD/AS diagram the main effects are shown by a shift left in
options: both the aggregate demand curve and the short-run aggregate supply curve.
the aggregate demand curve as consumers face higher prices for petrol.
the long-run aggregate supply curve as firms reduce their investment in renewable energy.
the short-run aggregate supply curve as firms face higher costs.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand curves (AD) and short-run aggregate supply curves (SRAS) for an economy. Which one of the following combinations of events is most likely to have caused the shift from AD1 to AD2 and the shift from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A fall in commodity prices and a fall in savings
A fall in money wages and an increase in imports
An increase in the budget deficit and a fall in productivity
An increase in VAT and an increase in income tax

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand curve (AD), short-run aggregate supply curve (SRAS), and long-run aggregate supply curve (LRAS) for an economy. The current level of real GDP is Y. Which one of the following policies is most likely, in the short run, to bring the economy closer to its normal capacity level of output?
options: An increase in the target rate of inflation
Higher government spending on vocational education
Lower rates of tax on manufacturing businesses
New schemes to encourage more household saving

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve, and two short-run aggregate supply (SRAS1 and SRAS2) curves for an economy. The economy’s initial equilibrium is at E1. The most likely explanation for the move of the economy from its initial equilibrium at E1 to a new short-run equilibrium at E2 is a decrease in the
options: level of tariffs on imports.
productivity of capital.
rate of wage inflation.
value of government subsidies to farmers.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) curve, the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve and the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve for an economy. The economy’s initial equilibrium is at E1. The government wants to achieve economic growth without conflicting with its long-run objective of price stability. All other things being equal, which one of the following policy combinations is most likely to enable the economy to achieve a new long-run equilibrium at E2?
options: A reduction in interest rates and increased government borrowing.
A reduction in the budget deficit and the rate of growth of the money supply.
Increased government expenditure on apprenticeships and transport infrastructure funded through borrowing.
Increased government expenditure on welfare funded through higher indirect taxes.

questions.questionText: In the diagram below, an economy is initially in equilibrium at point G. Aggregate demand then shifts from AD1 to AD2 and the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts from SRAS1 to SRAS2. Which one of the following combinations of events will cause these shifts in AD and SRAS and move the economy to a new equilibrium at point H?
options: A cut in income tax and an increase in VAT
A fall in money wages and a fall in house prices
An increase in productivity and a rise in consumer confidence
Higher energy prices and lower government expenditure

questions.questionText: An economy that imports most of its energy experiences a large appreciation in its exchange rate. Which one of the following AD/AS diagrams best illustrates the resulting changes to the economy’s price level and real national output?

The diagram below shows two aggregate demand (AD) curves and the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve for an economy. All other things being equal, the change in real national output from Y1 to Y2 is most likely to have been caused by an increase in the
options: government’s budget deficit.
level of interest rates.
size of the labour force.
volume of exports.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows two long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) and two short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is most likely to explain the movement to the right of both the short-run and long-run aggregate supply curves?
options: A large increase in the availability of renewable energy within the economy
An increase in employment and a depreciation of the exchange rate
An increase in the natural rate of unemployment and the level of money wage rates
A supply-side shock to the economy which increases the rate of inflation

questions.questionText: The diagrams below show the aggregate demand (AD) and short run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves for an economy. AD1 and SRAS1 show the initial positions of the curves and AD2 and SRAS2 the new positions. Which one of the following diagrams, A, B, C or D, illustrates a fall in world commodity prices as well as a fall in government spending?

The diagram below shows the initial short run aggregate supply curve (SRAS1) and long run aggregate supply curve (LRAS1) for an economy. SRAS2 and LRAS2 are the new positions of the two aggregate supply curves. The most likely combination of causes of the shifts in the short run and long run aggregate supply curves is
options: a fall in indirect tax and a fall in skill levels.
a fall in money wages and a rise in immigration.
a fall in productivity and a rise in emigration.
an increase in oil prices and more investment in renewable energy.

questions.questionText: The diagram below depicts an aggregate demand (AD) curve and two long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curves for an economy. The economy’s initial equilibrium is at E1. All other things being equal, the movement of the economy from its initial equilibrium at E1 to E2 is most likely to be caused by an increase in
options: government borrowing.
labour productivity.
the rate of deflation.
money wage rates.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows the aggregate demand (AD) and two short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curves for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is most likely to cause the short-run aggregate supply curve to shift from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A fall in the size of the labour force
An increase in imports
An increase in the value of the multiplier
Lower world commodity prices

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows two aggregate demand curves (AD) for an economy. All other things being equal, the most likely cause of the shift from AD1 to AD2 is an increase in
options: exports.
the rate of inflation.
interest rates.
the budget deficit.

questions.questionText: The diagram below shows two aggregate demand curves (AD) and the short-run aggregate supply curve (SRAS) for an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following is the most likely cause of the movement of the economy from equilibrium at Y1 to equilibrium at Y2?
options: A decrease in imports
An increase in savings
A decrease in the money supply
An increase in productivity

questions.questionText: An economy is in macroeconomic equilibrium, producing at its normal capacity level of output. Without long-run economic growth, a persistent increase in aggregate demand is likely to lead to an increase in the level of
options: real GDP.
employment.
productivity.
prices.

questions.questionText: The table below shows different sets of changes taking place in an economy. All other things being equal, which one of the following combinations, A, B, C or D, is most likely to have the effect of shifting the short-run aggregate supply curve for the economy to the left?

The diagram below shows two aggregate demand curves (AD) and two long-run aggregate supply curves (LRAS) for an economy. The economy’s initial equilibrium point is at E1. All other things being equal, which one of the following combinations of macroeconomic policies, A, B, C or D, is most likely to have moved the economy to its new equilibrium point at E2?
